headline: U.S. adds new checks on AI chips in Southeast Asia

chunks.text: A company does not need to own powerful computers. It can pay to use machines in another country online. Many Chinese companies have done this to {{work around}} American [[restrictions]] on [[advanced]] computer chips. On November 16, 2026, the U.S. moved to {{crack down on}} the [[practice]]. Its new rules add checks on chips sent to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

verbs.correct: To find a way to avoid a rule
verbs.wrong: To explain a rule to others
verbs.why: Some drivers work around the toll by taking small roads. People work around the limit by using a friend's account. Many Chinese companies have paid for computers abroad to work around American restrictions on chips.

verbs.correct: To act strongly to stop something
verbs.wrong: To build something in a factory
verbs.why: Police crack down on speeding near schools. The college cracks down on cheating during exams. On November 16, 2026, the United States moved to crack down on this way of using American chips.

chunks.text: Chips are small [[electronic parts]] that make computers work. The best ones help build artificial intelligence, or AI. Buildings full of computers are called [[data centers]]. Many have {{sprung up}} in Southeast Asia, and some {{rent out}} their [[computing power]], the ability to do many [[calculations]]. Renting let Chinese firms use chips they could not bring into China.

verbs.correct: To appear quickly in many places
verbs.why: New coffee shops spring up all over town. Food trucks spring up near the stadium every fall. Many data centers have sprung up in Southeast Asia.

verbs.correct: To let others pay to use something
verbs.wrong: To pay a debt little by little
verbs.why: My neighbors rent out their basement to a student. They rent out their beach house every summer. Some data centers in Southeast Asia rent out their computing power.

chunks.text: The U.S. has long tried to {{keep its best chips out}} of China, saying it must protect [[sensitive technology]]. The rules {{lay out}} two steps, and neither is a [[total ban]]. First, a [[license]], or [[official permission]], is needed to send certain advanced chips to the five countries. American companies can get the chips without one if they provide certain reports. U.S. officials say chips could otherwise {{wind up}} in China. Second, data centers worldwide need a license to sell large amounts of computing power to Chinese companies. Officials will decide whether to {{sign off on}} each [[request]].

verbs.wrong: To sell something at a low price
verbs.why: A tall fence keeps deer out of the garden. This heavy door keeps the cold air out. The United States has long tried to keep its best chips out of China.
The coach lays out the team rules on the first day. Her email lays out the plan for the week. The new rules lay out two main steps.
Lost socks often wind up under the bed. Most of our old clothes wind up at the thrift store. American officials say chips sent to the five countries could wind up in China.
The manager signs off on every vacation request. A senior doctor signs off on each new treatment plan. American officials will decide whether to sign off on each request.

chunks.text: On November 17, China accused the U.S. of misusing [[national security]] concerns. China's [[commerce ministry]] said it would {{fight back}} if the U.S. {{went ahead}}. The [[dispute]] came days before President Trump's [[planned meeting]] with China's President Xi. Singapore's prime minister said his country could manage the [[impact]]. Its officials were trying to {{figure out}} the rules. Malaysia said earlier it would not help firms avoid U.S. limits. Some experts say the rules could {{speed up}} China's work on its own chips.

verbs.correct: To answer an attack with action
verbs.wrong: To change the name of a product
verbs.why: When a bully pushes him, he fights back. The small company fights back when rivals attack its name. China's commerce ministry warned that China would fight back if the United States went ahead with the rules.
We go ahead with the picnic even when it is cloudy. The school goes ahead with the trip in light rain. China warned of action if the United States went ahead with the rules.
I can't figure out this new phone. She figures out the bus schedule in a few minutes. Officials in Singapore were trying to figure out the new rules.
A good map speeds up the trip. New machines speed up the work at the factory. Some experts say the rules could speed up China's work on its own chips.

mainIdea.s: The U.S. now requires licenses for some advanced chips sent to five countries and for big sales of computing power to Chinese firms. China has threatened to respond.
mainIdea.why: The rules cover both chip shipments and rented computing power. China warned that it would fight back if the United States went ahead.

mainIdea.s: New American rules order Southeast Asian governments to inspect every data center inside their borders. Officials there quickly agreed, and China accepts the plan.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the licenses apply to companies, not governments. China did not accept the rules, and it warned that it would fight back.

mainIdea.s: Several Asian nations have signed a trade deal to build their own computer chips together. The first factory will open in Malaysia next spring and create many jobs.
mainIdea.why: No such deal took place. The news is about American rules that crack down on renting advanced chips abroad and add checks on shipments.

tf.s: Chinese companies rented computing power abroad to work around U.S. restrictions.
tf.why: They paid to use chips in other countries, so they could use American chips they could not bring into China.

tf.s: The new U.S. rules are a total ban on sending AI chips to Southeast Asia.
tf.why: The rules require a license, and officials decide whether to sign off on each request.

tf.s: Data centers need a U.S. license to rent out a lot of computing power to Chinese firms.
tf.why: This applies to data centers anywhere in the world, and officials decide on each request.

tf.s: China said it would not fight back against the new U.S. rules.
tf.why: China's commerce ministry warned that it would fight back if the U.S. went ahead with them.

tf.s: Singapore said it was trying to figure out the new rules.
tf.why: Its prime minister also said the country could manage the impact.

tf.s: Some experts believe the rules will end China's work on its own chips.
tf.why: Some experts say the opposite could happen, because the rules could speed up that work.

lines.text: Did you see the new U.S. rules on AI chips?
I did, but [[what's the big deal]]? They're just computer parts.
They're the parts that make AI possible. Chinese companies were paying to use them in other countries to {{work around}} American restrictions.
There was a loophole, a gap in the law. Now the U.S. wants to {{crack down on}} it.
Why does it matter so much in Southeast Asia?
Huge data centers have {{sprung up}} there, and some {{rent out}} computing power to Chinese firms.
[[Not exactly]]. They need a U.S. license, and officials have to {{sign off on}} it.
So [[in theory]], they could still do business with China.
Right. But the U.S. is also worried that chips sent to the region could {{wind up}} in China.
It said it would {{fight back}} if the U.S. {{went ahead}}.
And these countries get [[caught in the crossfire]].
That's how it looks. Singapore is trying to {{figure out}} the rules.
They [[could backfire]]. Some experts say they could {{speed up}} China's work on its own chips.
